What we know on day 1,630 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia has banned voting against the war in September’s elections . The supreme court upheld a suit brought by a small pro-Kremlin nationalist party, Roblina, and stripped voters opposed to the war of their last option on the ballot: Yabloko, the country’s only remaining anti-war party . The court banned Yabloko’s entire list of federal election candidates from standing for the State Duma of Russia’s parliament. With most of Vladimir Putin’s opponents jailed, exiled or dead , Yabloko is the only liberal party still operating in Russia. Voting options other than Putin’s de facto party, the ruling United Russia, are only tolerated if they are too weak to win; give their backing to the Kremlin; or serve as “spoilers” that draw votes away from anyone who might pose a threat to the regime. About a hundred supporters, mostly young people, gathered outside the courthouse chanting “Shame! Shame!” after the ruling was delivered. Like the Duma, the supreme court routinely rubber-stamps the Kremlin’s wishes. Addressing protesters, Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov said the party would appeal against the decision. In an interview with Agence France-Presse on the weekend, Rybakov said about 40 party activists were facing prosecution for opposing the war. The party’s deputy leader, Maxim Kruglov, was jailed for seven years in June over social media posts, while Rybakov was fined and barred from elections for posting a photo of Alexei Navalny. Independent polls show most Russians favour peace negotiations with Kyiv . Russian ⁠missiles and ⁠aerial ​bombs killed five people and injured about 20 others in the ⁠south-eastern Ukrainian city ​of Zaporizhzhia ⁠early ‌on ‌Tuesday, said the ‌regional governor, Ivan Fedorov. At the same time, the military administration in Kyiv said warehouses in ​a central district ‌of the capital were ablaze after missile strikes. ‌One person was reported ‌injured. A Ukrainian MiG-29 fighter ⁠jet caught fire and crashed during ⁠a combat ⁠mission when a missile misfired, ​with the pilot ejecting safely. Ukraine’s air force said the ‌pilot – who had been targeting ‌Russian positions in ‌the southern region of Odesa – was taken ‌to hospital. Russia’s rollout of a Starlink alternative to counteract its banning from the US-based system is taking place faster than predicted, with 16 satellites in orbit so far , top Ukrainian intelligence official Maj Gen ‌Vadym Skibitskyi has warned. Russia’s Rassvet system remains a far cry from Starlink, which had more than 10,000 satellites as of June and has given Kyiv a major advantage in drone operations and battlefield communications. Speaking to RBC-Ukraine, Skibitskyi, head of the Ukrainian GUR, said Rassvet has “begun launching ‌it much faster than originally planned”. Russia planned to have 292 satellites by 2027 and ‌924 by 2035. “Once Russia deploys a full satellite constellation, the system will operate like Starlink. Discussions are ​already under way on how to counter it.” Analysts have noted that while Russia has been slow to produce innovations in the war, it is quick to adapt to and copy Ukraine’s actions, introducing corresponding systems that it produces and adopts rapidly. As Russia pounds Ukraine with supersonic missiles that Ukrainians have no interceptors for, Skibitskyi said Moscow had already met its annual ⁠production targets for Zircon and Oniks missiles in the first seven ​months of 2026 ​and was exceeding its 2026 ​missile production goals by 10% to 20%. At the same time, Ukraine’s emerging ​ballistic missile industry, and drone ​production facilities, had ​become a priority target for Russia’s missile campaign. Russia’s stockpile of Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the mainstay of its supersonic strikes, was estimated at about 130, with 65 new ones made in July alone. On Tuesday, there were unconfirmed reports that Russian ballistic missile launcher systems were destroyed inside Russia, not far from the border. Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13 Read more A Ukrainian drone strike set fire to the Taneco refinery in the Russian city of Nizhnekamsk , about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border, Luke Harding writes . Ukraine’s general staff said it was part of a campaign to reduce the “military potential of the Russian aggressor”. Russian authorities said at least 13 people were killed. Taneco is one of Russia’s biggest and most technologically advanced oil refineries, and part of it produces rubber and petrochemical products. Overnight into Monday, Ukraine’s armed forces hit equipment depots and a repair unit in the occupied Donetsk and Luhansk parts of eastern Ukraine , while ⁠Russian-installed local authorities said the ⁠Zaporizhzhia region in south-east Ukraine was largely without ⁠electricity on Monday ⁠after ​Ukrainian attacks destroyed key power facilities. Reuters reports that Ukraine is considering shipping grain by rail through Moldova as a more ⁠secure export option than by ⁠sea as its ports are battered by Russian attacks. Sources in Ukraine and Moldova said Kyiv wants a 50% discount on freight through Moldova to the Romanian port of Constanța. A source at Moldovan Railways said Moldova wants guarantees about the volume to be transported. The Ukrainians estimate a working corridor could provide for 10% of Ukraine’s exports. Moldovan and Ukrainian ministers met in Odesa on Monday for discussions. Photograph: Kimmo Brandt/EPA Estonia Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine European and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in Tallinn Europe live – latest updates Jon Henley Europe correspondent and agencies Tue 29 Sep 2026 10.20 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google European and Nato leaders have expressed full support for Estonia and Ukraine after the Baltic state said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on social media on Tuesday that such attacks were “absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the Estonian capital, Tallinn, was being summoned to his ministry. Estonia’s national security agency said a fire broke out on 15 August at a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which makes unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine. Two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia on 17 August, followed by a third the next day. All three were handed over to Estonia, it said. Tsahkna said the subsequent investigation had led authorities to “conclude with certainty” that the attack was “an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation”. It was part of a “broader campaign across Europe aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine”, he said. Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal, said his country’s response to Russia’s campaign would “be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia . We will not be intimidated.” Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and, along with its fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, has significantly increased its defence spending. Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Estonia’s allegations were “unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever”. He said Russia “cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t”. Western allies pledged their continued support to Estonia and Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels, Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies”, adding that it was “failing … on the battlefield in Ukraine, and failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine”. Speaking alongside Rutte, Lithuania’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said Russia’s actions were becoming “increasingly hostile and less restrained … We see the hybrid attacks – in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now, it’s a question of Russia’s actions.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Ukraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in Russia Read more Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Russia’s fingerprints were “all over” the Tallinn attack, while the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, said further support for Ukraine “will be needed, and must be provided”. The EU said it stood with Estonia, describing the arson attack as “reckless” and saying it would not be put off supporting Ukraine. “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen,” a European Commission spokesperson said. France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called the arson attack a “dangerous escalation”. Moscow “needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine”, Macron said on social media. Sweden’s acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called Estonia’s formal attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said the UK “stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.” About 200 incidents of suspected Russian sabotage and malign activity have been recorded across Europe since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including arson plots at warehouses, drone incursions, thefts of defence technology and cyber-attacks on essential European infrastructure.
